passage: Tarun's father had been in the district hospital in Satara for four days, and Tarun, twenty-five, was running between the ward and their village forty minutes away. He couldn't sleep. He kept checking his phone for bad news. On the fifth morning, Farida, who ran the medical shop near the bus stand, found him staring at the ceiling fan. "Write two lists," she said, handing him a receipt pad. He did. In my hands: bring clean clothes, ask the doctor my questions at the evening round, keep the cows fed, eat something, sleep. Not in my hands: how fast Baba heals, what the tests show. He stared at the second list for a long time. Then he folded it and put it in his pocket. That night he fed the cows, ate two rotis, and slept for six hours without checking his phone once.

qa.a: Forty minutes away.

qa.a: He was anxious and exhausted, unable to sleep and constantly checking his phone for bad news.

qa.a: He would have a son who is rested and clear when asking the doctor questions at the evening round, instead of one worn out by worry.

grounding: Shows a young adult worried about his father's health doing what he can and releasing the rest, which eases his suffering.

passage: Daniel had spent eight months on the grant application for his community-garden project in Porto. On Friday he clicked submit at 4:58 pm, two minutes before the deadline. The decision would take six weeks. That weekend he refreshed his email forty times. On Sunday, Beatriz found him rereading the budget table. "Did you do everything you could?" she asked. He thought. "I checked every number. I asked three people to review it. I got the letters of support." "Then what's left?" "Waiting." "And is waiting yours to do anything about?" He laughed, a bit tired. "No." Beatriz tossed him his swimming bag. "Then let's go to the sea." At the beach he still thought about the grant, but he didn't refresh anything. For six weeks he worked on the garden with the kids, grant or no grant.

qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.a: He was anxious and restless, refreshing his email forty times and rereading the budget table.

qa.a: She asked what was still his to do, then took him to the sea, helping him release the waiting he couldn't control.

qa.a: They got his full attention on the garden for six weeks, instead of a distracted Daniel checking email.

passage: In the surgery waiting room of the city hospital in Kolkata, Samir couldn't sit still. His mother had gone in at nine. It was now eleven thirty. He paced, checked the board, asked the nurse twice. His sister Swati pulled him onto the bench. "Samir. What can we actually do right now?" He opened his mouth to say "nothing" and stopped. "We can call Mama and tell him. We can eat something. We can make sure the forms are signed." "And what can't we do?" He swallowed. "The surgery." "So let's do our list." Samir called Mama. Swati got two cups of tea and a packet of biscuits. They signed the last form at the desk. When they sat down again, Samir didn't pace. He still watched the doors, but his hands were still. At one fifteen, the doctor came out smiling.

qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as he paced and checked the board?
qa.a: Samir was anxious and restless, unable to sit still while waiting.

qa.a: Asking what they could actually do turned helpless waiting into a short list of actions, which calmed Samir.

qa.q: How might Swati have been feeling while helping her brother?
qa.a: She was probably worried too, but steadier, and chose to help them both through the wait.

grounding: Shows a young adult waiting during a parent's surgery separating what is in his hands from what is not, which reduces his suffering.

Tejas keeps saying he's let go of Pallavi. "It's done, I'm totally over it, I've moved on." He said it three times at dinner tonight.

When my Nani let go of the old house, she talked about it easily, even laughed about the leaking roof. That was calm. This is not.

Mohit

Kindergarten note, Thursday.
While I was talking with Gurpreet's mother at pickup, Avni (5) ran up and tugged my sleeve. "Ma'am! Ma'am! My tooth is wobbly! Look!" She did it three times. When I said, "Wait, Avni," her face crumpled and she said, "But I'll forget!"

qa.a: She was probably a little distracted but likely amused, seeing how excited Avni was.

passage: In the courtyard of their village house near Hubli, Mehak, five, was playing with the new kittens. Her big brother Karthik called from the doorway, "Mehak, wash your hands, lunch is ready!" Mehak kept stroking the kittens. "Mehak! Lunch!" Nothing. Karthik walked over, crouched down beside her, and said, "Mehak," and waited until she looked at him. Then, softly: "Wash your hands now. Lunch." Mehak blinked. "Oh! Okay!" She put down the kitten and ran to the tap.

qa.q: What was Mehak playing with?
qa.a: The new kittens.

qa.q: Why didn't Mehak respond the first two times?
qa.a: She was so absorbed and happy with the kittens that she heard the voice but didn't take in the words.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that worked?
qa.a: He crouched to her level, said her name, waited until she looked at him, and then spoke.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt after calling twice?
qa.a: He was probably a little frustrated at first, but found a calm way to get her attention.

grounding: Shows a young child who hears an instruction while absorbed in play and doesn't process it, until an adult gets to eye level and uses her name first.

passage: In their London flat, Elif, four, was building a tall tower of blocks. Her father, Emeka, called from the kitchen, "Elif, put your shoes on, we're going to the park." Elif added another block. "Elif, shoes!" She didn't look up. Emeka came over and knelt beside her. "Elif." She looked at him. "Shoes on, then the park." Elif's eyes went wide. "The park? Yay!" She left the tower and ran for her shoes.

qa.q: What was Elif building?
qa.a: A tall tower of blocks.

qa.q: What does Elif's wide-eyed 'The park? Yay!' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was excited and hadn't really heard about the park before, because her attention was on the tower.

qa.q: What worked better than calling from the kitchen?
qa.a: Kneeling beside her and saying her name first, so she looked at him before he gave the instruction.

qa.q: How might Emeka feel when Elif finally hears him?
qa.a: He might feel relieved and amused that she was so happy once she actually heard the plan.

grounding: Shows a child who hears a parent's instruction while focused on a toy but doesn't process it, until the parent gets to her level and uses her name.

passage: At the preschool in Ahmedabad, Shankar sir said to the class, "Everyone, put your crayons in the box and come to the mat." Most children moved. Aparna, five, kept colouring her elephant, lost in it. Shankar sir said it again. Nothing. He walked over, knelt down beside her, and said, "Aparna." She looked up. "Crayons in the box, then the mat." Aparna looked at the empty tables in surprise. "Oh!" She dropped her crayons in the box and hurried over.

qa.q: What was Aparna colouring?
qa.a: An elephant.

qa.q: How did Aparna seem to feel when she noticed the empty tables?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and a little startled, not having noticed the class moving.

qa.q: What small step helped Aparna follow the instruction?
qa.a: Shankar sir knelt beside her and said her name first, getting her attention before repeating the instruction.

qa.q: How might the other children see Aparna staying at the table?
qa.a: They may not notice much, or they may think she was just busy colouring.

grounding: Shows a child who hears an instruction while absorbed in her colouring and does not process it, until a teacher kneels and says her name.

passage:
Tuesday night
Had a fight with Varun today. He said, "You always take the bigger piece of cake." And before he even finished I was saying, "No I don't! Last week YOU took the bigger piece!"
Then he said, "I'm not talking about cake, I mean you never let me choose anything." And I said, "That's not true, I let you choose the movie on Sunday!"
Then he went quiet and went to his room.
Now I'm lying here thinking. I heard every word he said, but I was only listening for the bits I could argue with. I didn't really hear what he meant. I think he meant he feels left out.
Tomorrow I'll ask him what he meant, and just listen.
Ankita

qa.q: What did Varun say Ankita always takes?
qa.a: The bigger piece of cake.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling while lying in bed thinking about the fight?
qa.a: Ankita felt sorry and a bit guilty, realising the listening was only to argue and missing that Varun felt left out.

qa.q: What small step does Ankita plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: To ask Varun what he meant and simply listen, without arguing back.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt when Ankita kept arguing?
qa.a: He probably felt unheard and frustrated, which is why he went quiet and left.

grounding: Shows a child hearing a sibling's words only enough to defend and correct, missing what he really meant.

passage: Irawati came running to the well in their village near Pune, out of breath. "Aparna, my goat got out and ate the neighbour's bajra. Aai was so angry, and—" "Goats don't eat bajra," Aparna interrupted. "They eat leaves." "No, listen, this one did, and Aai said—" "It must have been your fault. You didn't tie the rope properly." Irawati's face fell. She stopped talking and started pulling up the bucket. Aparna kept going, explaining how to tie a knot. Irawati didn't answer. Walking home, Aparna wondered why her friend had gone so quiet. Then she remembered Irawati's face when she said "Aai was so angry." She hadn't even let her finish. The next morning, Aparna waited at the well. "Irawati, what happened with your Aai?" This time she listened to the end.

qa.q: What did Irawati's goat eat?
qa.a: The neighbour's bajra.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: Aparna felt puzzled at first, then regretful, realising she hadn't let her friend finish.

qa.q: What did Aparna do differently the next morning?
qa.a: She asked Irawati what happened with her Aai and listened to the end instead of correcting her.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when Aparna kept correcting her?
qa.a: Irawati felt hurt and unheard, so she went quiet and pulled up the bucket.

grounding: Shows a child hearing a friend only enough to correct and blame, missing the worry underneath, then trying to listen better.

passage: At recess in their Nairobi school, Wanjiru sat beside Camila on the bench. "You didn't save me a seat at lunch yesterday," Wanjiru said quietly. "I felt—" "I did save one! Zawadi sat in it before I could stop her," Camila said quickly. "It wasn't my fault." "I'm not saying it's your fault. I'm saying I felt—" "And you were late anyway, so I thought you weren't coming." Wanjiru looked away. "Forget it." She got up and went to the swings. Camila sat alone, confused. Then she replayed it. Wanjiru had said "I felt" twice, and Camila had jumped in both times. She had heard only the part she could defend. At the end of recess, Camila went to the swings. "Wanjiru, how did you feel?" Wanjiru looked at her. "Left out," she said. Camila nodded, and this time she didn't argue.

qa.q: Who sat in the seat Camila said she saved?
qa.a: Zawadi.

qa.q: What did Camila realise as she replayed the conversation?
qa.a: Camila felt confused and then regretful, realising she had jumped in twice to defend herself and never let Wanjiru say how she felt.

qa.q: What did Camila do differently at the end of recess?
qa.a: She asked Wanjiru how she felt and listened without arguing.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru feel about the lunch seat?
qa.a: She felt left out.

grounding: Shows a child listening only enough to defend herself, missing her friend's feelings until she stops and asks.

passage:
"Ira, beta, you're staring at your phone like it owes you money," said Reena aunty, sitting on the swing. "Let me tell you something. When I was fifteen, my family was moving from Shimla to Delhi, and I was terrified. New school, no friends. I told my friend Sheetal on our last walk. She was holding a book she loved, and she closed it. Put it down on the bench. And she said, 'What scares you most about it?'
Nobody else had asked me that. My parents said it would be fine. My teacher said I'd make friends. Sheetal just asked, and then listened.
I cried a bit, told her about the lunchroom, the bus, everything. She didn't fix anything. But I felt like I mattered. I still remember that book on the bench, forty years later."

qa.q: What did Sheetal do with her book?
qa.a: She closed it and put it down on the bench.

qa.q: How did young Reena feel when Sheetal asked what scared her most?
qa.a: She felt truly heard and that she mattered, since no one else had asked.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Reena aunty's story?
qa.a: Sheetal putting the book down and asking a real question, which let Reena share her fears and feel heard.

qa.q: How might Sheetal have felt listening to Reena's fears?
qa.a: She probably felt sad about her friend leaving, but cared enough to put her book aside and listen.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how a friend putting a book down and asking a follow-up question made her feel truly heard as a teenager.

passage: The school bus was packed and the driver had the radio blaring when Anand finally said it to Nitin. "I think I'm getting dropped from the hockey team." Nitin was scrolling through videos. Anand sighed and looked out the window. Then he noticed: Nitin had put his phone face-down on his knee. "Wait, what? Why do you think that?" Anand was surprised. "Coach moved me to the reserves for the last two matches. And he didn't say anything." "That's rough. Did you ask him?" "No. I'm scared he'll say yes." "Want to go together tomorrow before practice?" Anand stared at the phone on Nitin's knee. It stayed there until their stop. Nitin didn't have a magic answer. But getting off the bus, Anand felt lighter than he had all week.

qa.q: How many matches had Anand been moved to the reserves for?
qa.a: The last two matches.

qa.q: What did Anand feel when he noticed Nitin's phone was face-down?
qa.a: He felt surprised and then that he mattered, because Nitin had set aside his phone to really listen.

qa.q: What small step did Nitin offer?
qa.a: To go with Anand to talk to Coach before practice tomorrow.

qa.q: What would change if Nitin had kept scrolling?
qa.a: Anand might have felt ignored and kept the worry to himself, feeling more alone.

grounding: Shows a teenager sharing a worry and feeling truly heard when a friend puts his phone down and asks a follow-up question.

passage: At the colony park in Lucknow, Asif sat on the swings with Damini after tuition. Damini was texting. "My Nani keeps forgetting things," Asif said, without looking up. "Yesterday she called me by my father's name." Damini's thumbs stopped. She put her phone in her pocket. "That sounds scary. How are you feeling about it?" Asif looked at her. He'd told two other friends, and both had said, "Oh, old people forget," and gone back to their phones. "Scared," he said. "She taught me to read." "Does your family know?" "Ammi's taking her to the doctor on Saturday." Damini nodded. "Can I check on you after?" Asif felt his throat tighten. He nodded. They swung quietly until the streetlights came on.

qa.q: What did Nani call Asif yesterday?
qa.a: By his father's name.

qa.q: How did Asif feel when Damini put her phone away?
qa.a: He felt surprised and truly heard, since his other friends had brushed it off, and his throat tightened with feeling.

qa.q: What did Damini do that made Asif feel he mattered?
qa.a: She stopped texting, put her phone away, and asked how he was feeling, then offered to check on him after Saturday.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt listening to Asif?
qa.a: She probably felt concerned for him and caring, which is why she offered to check in.

grounding: Shows a teenager sharing a worry and feeling he matters when a friend puts her phone away and asks a follow-up question.
